\sphinxAtStartPar
GATOH is a Python package that provides a framework for creating complex, multilayer
agent\sphinxhyphen{}based models.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is licensed under the \sphinxhref{license.html}{MIT} license, and the source code is hosted on
GitHub at:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxurl{https://github.com/JungleHollow/GATOH}

\section{What is GATOH?}
\label{\detokenize{user/whatisgatoh:what-is-gatoh}}\label{\detokenize{user/whatisgatoh:whatisgatoh}}\label{\detokenize{user/whatisgatoh::doc}}

\section{Installing GATOH}
\label{\detokenize{user/installation:installing-gatoh}}\label{\detokenize{user/installation:installation}}\label{\detokenize{user/installation::doc}}

\section{GATOH Quickstart}
\label{\detokenize{user/quickstart:gatoh-quickstart}}\label{\detokenize{user/quickstart::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The Generalised Agent Transformation of Opinions in Hierarchies, or GATOH, framework is an agent\sphinxhyphen{}based modeling library
for Python. It is designed to provide a highly flexible and generalisable framework that can define and simulate a wide
variety of agent\sphinxhyphen{}based models centered on opinion dynamics.


\subsection{Installing GATOH}
\label{\detokenize{user/quickstart:installing-gatoh}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
GATOH has been primarily developed and tested on a x86\_64 Linux system, but support for 64 bit Windows has also been
confirmed. The different methods for installing GATOH are outlined below:

\begin{sphinxuseclass}{sphinx-tabs}
\sphinxAtStartPar
From source
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ensure that Python \textgreater{}=3.14 is installed on your system.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Clone the library’s code from the git repository: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git clone https://github.com/JungleHollow/GATOH}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If needed, create a virtual environment to install the library to.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
From the target python environment, simply install GATOH using pip as normal, but specify the path to the GATOH directory rather than the package name: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{python \sphinxhyphen{}m pip install \textless{}path to GATOH directory\textgreater{}}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
At this point, all required dependencies will be installed alongside GATOH, and you can begin using the library.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
PyPi
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ensure that Python \textgreater{}= 3.14 is installed on your system.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
…

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Work in progress}

\end{sphinxuseclass}

\subsection{Using GATOH}
\label{\detokenize{user/quickstart:using-gatoh}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Once you have installed GATOH, you can use it by importing gatoh in your python scripts. Almost all functions and classes in GATOH are
currently organised into their own submodules, meaning that these will need to be imported and used accordingly. Below is a simple
example of what very basic GATOH usage could look like:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{gatoh}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{model}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{ABModel}
\PYG{k+kn}{from}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nn}{gatoh}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{utils}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{plot\PYGZus{}graph}

\PYG{n}{HIERARCHIES} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Religious}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Neighbours}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Family}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Friends}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{n}{HIERARCHY\PYGZus{}RW} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
    \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Religious}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.3}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Neighbours}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Family}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.01}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Friends}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{n}{model} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{ABModel}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{HIERARCHIES}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{HIERARCHY\PYGZus{}RW}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{iterations}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{model\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{TEST\PYGZus{}MODEL}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{generate\PYGZus{}agents}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{TEST}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
        \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{neutral}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.4}\PYG{p}{,}
        \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{social}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.4}\PYG{p}{,}
        \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{impulsive}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.2}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{number}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{20}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{generate\PYGZus{}graphs}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{HIERARCHIES}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{agents}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{method}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{blockmodel}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{agent\PYGZus{}subsetting}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{iterate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{x\PYGZus{}vals} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{iterations}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i} \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{i} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{range}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{n}{y\PYGZus{}vals} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{aggregate\PYGZus{}opinions}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{n}{model}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{logger}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{variables}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{aggregate\PYGZus{}opinions}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{n}{plot\PYGZus{}graph}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{x\PYGZus{}vals}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{y\PYGZus{}vals}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{o}{.}
\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can refer to the {\hyperref[\detokenize{user/basics::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Basic tutorial}}}} for more information on how to use GATOH,

\section{GATOH: The absolute basics for beginners}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:gatoh-the-absolute-basics-for-beginners}}\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners::doc}}

\subsection{Prerequisites}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:prerequisites}}\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:user-abs-beginners}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A basic knowledge of Python is assumed. For further reference, see the \sphinxhref{https://docs.python.org/tutorial/}{Python tutorial}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
To work the examples, you’ll need the \sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH} (Generalised Agent Transformation of Opinions in Hierarchies) framework and its included dependencies installed.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Learner Profile}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is a quick overview of agent\sphinxhyphen{}based modelling, and its implementation in \sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH}. It demonstrates how agents are defined, and how they
interact with each other and their environment to produce emergent behaviours. If you are looking for a basic introduction to \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} (Agent\sphinxhyphen{}Based Modelling) principles in the
\sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH} framework, then this article may be of use to you.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Learning Objectives}

\sphinxAtStartPar
After reading, you should be able to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand what an “agent” is, and how they are defined;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand the basic process of \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} from start to finish;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand the different use\sphinxhyphen{}cases for \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM};

\end{itemize}


\subsection{The Basics}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:the-basics}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To start with, the fundamental modelling method that \sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH} is based around is that of \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM}. The implementation of
\sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABMs} (Agent\sphinxhyphen{}Based Models) can be approached in a variety of ways depending on the nature of the scenario that they are simulating.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The scenario must be properly defined \textendash{} and there must be a clear idea of the type of behaviours that emerge from the scenario, as well as who or what
produces those behaviours. It is also important to consider the environment in the scenario, and whether or not it has a significant
impact on the emergent behaviours.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH} is primarily designed with sociological or anthropological simulations in mind. The simplest general scenario that is intended
to be modelled with \sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH} is that of social contagion in some community or social network; with the emergent behaviour in this scenario
being the spread of some idea or belief between the people who live in the community.

\sphinxAtStartPar
But, social interactions between community members are not simple, and are heavily influenced by a number of factors \textendash{} primarily the different social hierarchies that exist in the
community, that agents may or may not belong to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the next sections, we will explore the different components that make up a \sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH} model, and the ways that they interact with
each other.


\subsubsection{Agent\sphinxhyphen{}Based Modelling}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:agent-based-modelling}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} is a computational modelling strategy that has grown in popularity in recent years as computer
hardware has become more powerful.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABMs} were simple, cell\sphinxhyphen{}based systems, where each cell represented a single agent. The most famous
example of these types of \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABMs} is Conway’s Game of Life\DUrole{bibtex-citation}{{[}\hyperlink{cite.user/abs_beginners:id6}{1}{]}} . In this rudimentary
\sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM}, simple rules are defined which determine how and when each cell ‘comes to life’ or ‘dies’ based
on the cell’s current state, and the state of its immediate neighbours.

\sphinxAtStartPar
From these simple rules, relatively complex behaviours can emerge.
In the depiction below, we can see some examples of the behaviours that can emerge from such a simple system:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
          ================================================================
          ║            Conway\textquotesingle{}s Game of Life (1970):                     ║
          ================================================================
          ║ Still life patterns:   ⫼          Oscillators:               ║
          ================================================================
          ║┌─╥─╥─╥─┐   ┌─╥─╥─╥─┐   ⫼                                     ║
          ║│ ║ ║ ║ │   │ ║ ║ ║ │   ⫼   ┌─╥─╥─┐   ┌─╥─╥─┐   ┌─╥─╥─┐       ║
          ║╞═╬═╬═╬═╡   ╞═╬═╬═╬═╡   ⫼   │ ║ ║ │   │ ║█║ │   │ ║ ║ │       ║
          ║│ ║█║█║ │   │ ║█║█║ │   ⫼   ╞═╬═╬═╡   ╞═╬═╬═╡   ╞═╬═╬═╡       ║
          ║╞═╬═╬═╬═╡ \(\rightarrow\) ╞═╬═╬═╬═╡   ⫼   │█║█║█│ \(\rightarrow\) │ ║█║ │ \(\rightarrow\) │█║█║█│ \(\rightarrow\)  ...║
          ║│ ║█║█║ │   │ ║█║█║ │   ⫼   ╞═╬═╬═╡   ╞═╬═╬═╡   ╞═╬═╬═╡       ║
          ║╞═╬═╬═╬═╡   ╞═╬═╬═╬═╡   ⫼   │ ║ ║ │   │ ║█║ │   │ ║ ║ │       ║
          ║│ ║ ║ ║ │   │ ║ ║ ║ │   ⫼   └─╨─╨─┘   └─╨─╨─┘   └─╨─╨─┘       ║
          ║└─╨─╨─╨─┘   └─╨─╨─╨─┘   ⫼                                     ║
          ================================================================
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Whilst it was revolutionary at its time of creation, the Game of Life was developed in a context where computers were still in their infancy,
and they were still basically just a step above calculators. To give an example, the Cray\sphinxhyphen{}1 \textendash{} a 5.5 ton supercomputer released in 1976 \textendash{} had
a processor capable of running 80 million operations per second, and had 8.4 megabytes of memory available.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now, in 2026, the newest consumer \sphinxstyleabbreviation{CPUs} (Computer Processing Units) are capable of performing around 5 billion operations per second, and they
have more memory available in just their L3 cache than 20 Cray\sphinxhyphen{}1 supercomputers would have had collectively in the 1970s(!). Considering this,
it is easy to see how \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABMs} would have started evolving past these simple 2\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional, binary cells in the following
decades.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now it is possible to model extremely complex systems such as the spread of global pandemics, or the nature of peak\sphinxhyphen{}hour traffic in a large city.
Although \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} can be applied to many use\sphinxhyphen{}cases, there is still some care that must be taken when creating such models.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each area of interest has very specific characterisations, rules, and interactions, which must all be appropriately quantified and defined for the model
to be representative of real life. Using the examples of global pandemics and car traffic, we can see that models for these scenarios would have inherently
different approaches.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A model that simulates a global pandemic might treat interactions between agents as the driving force that spreads the ‘emergent behaviour’
(as interactions between agents would enable viral transmissions), whereas the ‘interaction’ between agents in a traffic model would in itself be the emergent
behaviour (as the ‘interaction’ of a large number of agents would imply that traffic has built up).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the purposes of this guide, let’s look at another famous \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} from the same era as Conway’s game of life \textendash{} Schelling’s
model of segregation \DUrole{bibtex-citation}{{[}\hyperlink{cite.user/abs_beginners:id8}{2}{]}}. In the following sections, we will break down \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABMs} into their core components,
and see how each fits into the overall modeling process; using Schelling’s model as an example.


\subsubsection{Defining the problem}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:defining-the-problem}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The first, and arguably most important, step in the agent\sphinxhyphen{}based modeling process is the concrete definition of the problem and its computational representation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the problem is not defined correctly from the start, then this just leads to a lot of headache and time lost further along the line, as any changes that have
to be made later \textendash{} no matter how minor or isolated they may appear \textendash{} will likely be connected to a number of other components that will have to be redefined
and tweaked as well.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is particularly important when we are talking about highly complicated models that take multiple hours to run \sphinxstyleemphasis{one} iteration; it’s not
a great experience when you realise that a model parameter is wrong and has to be changed when your model is halfway done with its iterations and has already been
running for the past week…

\sphinxAtStartPar
All of this to say that it is very important and worthwhile to spend some extra time at the start to think through, and properly define the representation of the
problem for your model.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the case of Schelling’s model of segregation, the foundation of the model is based on the assumption that no outside influences or explicit prejudices exist (
for the purposes of the model); with the only factor affecting possible segregation being the presence of “mild in\sphinxhyphen{}group preferences” in people. Following this
assumption, the model is defined as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A community is represented by a \(N \times N\) grid of cells.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Each cell in the community represents a space that can be inhabitted by an agent, or be empty.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Every agent in the community is assigned to one of two “groups”.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
At every iteration, each agent:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Observes its immediate neighbours (ignoring empty spaces).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the proportion of neighbours belonging to the same “group” is equal or greater to some threshold, the agent is content and remains stationary.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Otherwise, the agent is dissatisfied, and will move from its current space to another empty space in the community.

\end{enumerate}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this way, a seemingly complex problem (such as racial segregation in the case of Schelling) can be defined in a more deterministic manner that can be more easily
managed computationally.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In some cases, this may mean a simplification (i.e. reducing the level of detail of, or completely removing a concept from the model), whilst
in other cases this may mean having to think outside the box a bit to be able to quantify some property or behaviour that by nature isn’t already quantified (e.g.
treating the strength of a person’s beliefs as a value on a scale from 0\sphinxhyphen{}10).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{Schellings}.png}
\caption{\sphinxstylestrong{Fig.} Schelling’s model of segregation in action\sphinxfootnotemark[*]}\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:id66}}\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Above, I have included a short GIF (if viewing in HTML) depicting the runtime of Schelling’s model of segregation so that you can understand better how everything will fit together.
As you can see, the agents start in a relatively random distribution within the community, but as more iterations happen, the community slowly becomes more
and more segregated into distinct “tribes”.


\subsubsection{Agents}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:agents}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition:} An agent is an entity that is capable of acting without external input, and can interact with other agents and the environment
around it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
One of the core objects of the \sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH} framework is the “Agent”. In the \sphinxstyleabbreviation{GATOH}
framework, an Agent represents an “average” person that lives in some community, and interacts with their neighbours in different social contexts.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Agents can be defined in a number of different ways depending on the exact nature of the problem, but there is rarely an ‘optimal’ definition; each alternative has its own pros and cons.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The core definition of an agent will obviously vary depending on the problem definition, as different types of problems will be interested in tracking and simulating different types of characteristics
or traits in their agents. For example, if the model is being constructed to simulate car traffic, each agent might represent an individual car on the streets.

\sphinxAtStartPar
But even if the problem definition remains fixed, there are multiple ways of defining agents. If a model is instead simulating the spread of avian flu in birds, each agent could represent a single bird,
or a flock of birds that are migrating in an area. In this way, the exact definition of the agents in the model will have an impact on what exactly happens when different “agents” interact with each
other; as the interaction can be representative of individual or group effects.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Another thing to keep in mind when defining an agent is how, or if, the agent will interact with the space around them (if there even is a “space” defined for your particular model).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Depending on the mechanism that you have chosen to use for agent\sphinxhyphen{}space interaction, it may be necessary for agents to hold additional attributes so that they can differentiate the information that
they provide for agent\sphinxhyphen{}agent interactions versus agent\sphinxhyphen{}space interactions, as these will likely not involve the same behaviours:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
          ================================================================
          ║                Example Held Attributes                       ║
          ================================================================
          ║          Agent           ⫼          Agent (with space)       ║
          ================================================================
          ║    \sphinxhyphen{} Name                ⫼    \sphinxhyphen{} Name                         ║
          ║    \sphinxhyphen{} Age                 ⫼    \sphinxhyphen{} Age                          ║
          ║                          ⫼    \sphinxhyphen{} X coordinate                 ║
          ║                          ⫼    \sphinxhyphen{} Y coordinate                 ║
          ║                          ⫼    \sphinxhyphen{} Travel distance              ║
          ║                          ⫼    \sphinxhyphen{} Travel probability           ║
          ║                          ⫼    \sphinxhyphen{} Travel frequency             ║
          ================================================================
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In the case of Schelling’s model of segregation, an agent represents a person that lives within some arbitrary community, and they may belong to one of two different groups. The agents in Schelling’s model do not
“interact” with each other in the traditional sense, but rather they observe the traits of their neighbours.

\sphinxAtStartPar
These agents do, however, interact with the space around them; moving from their current cells to empty ones if they are not satisfied with the group makeup of their neighbours.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Although, in this particular case no additional information is needed to differentiate between agent\sphinxhyphen{}agent and agent\sphinxhyphen{}space interactions, as each cell contains all the needed information
(either the agent’s group if the cell is occupied, or nothing if the cell is empty).


\subsubsection{Model Space}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:model-space}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The model “space” was briefly touched on in the previous section, but let’s look at it in some more detail here.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Just how we live in and interact with the space around us (our homes, neighbourhoods, cities, etc.) an agent in an \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} may interact with some form of “space” around them if the model
requires it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For some models, space is a core factor for the emergent behaviour \textendash{} it would be impossible to simulate the presence of car traffic if agents had no space to create traffic in, for instance.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In other models, space is simply a way of capturing additional information; the inclusion of “space” and “distance” may allow for a stronger, more accurate model, but the underlying behaviours that are being simulated do not
directly depend on the space itself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
And of course, it may be possible for some models to not require a “space” at all.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similarly to how there are many ways of defining an agent, each with their own pros and cons, there are many ways of defining model space.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The model space can be an explicit “map” with coordinates that the agents inhabit:
\begin{sphinxalltt}
                      =========================================
                      ║          Map\sphinxhyphen{}based model space:       ║
                      =========================================
                      ║        ┌─────╥─────╥─────╥─────┐      ║
                      ║        │(0,y)║(1,y)║(...)║(x,y)│      ║
                      ║        ╞═════╬═════╬═════╬═════╡      ║
                      ║        │(...)║(...)║(...)║(...)│      ║
                      ║        ╞═════╬═════╬═════╬═════╡      ║
                      ║        │(0,1)║(1,1)║(...)║(x,1)│      ║
                      ║        ╞═════╬═════╬═════╬═════╡      ║
                      ║        │(0,0)║(1,0)║(...)║(x,0)│      ║
                      ║        └─────╨─────╨─────╨─────┘      ║
                      =========================================
\end{sphinxalltt}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Or it could follow a graph\sphinxhyphen{}based approach instead:

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\capstart

\noindent\sphinxincludegraphics{{HierarchiesExample_Universal}.png}
\caption{\sphinxstylestrong{Fig.} A depiction of a graph\sphinxhyphen{}based model space}\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:id67}}\end{figure}

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also possible for model space to be more of an abstract concept; with agents posessing attributes that note the different cities that they live in, for example.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For Schelling’s model, a \(N \times N\) cell grid is used, where \(N \times N\) must be greater than the total number of agents to allow for agents to move into empty cells. Schelling’s model is somewhat different to
the “traditional” \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} when it comes to the model space, with the cells doubling as both the spaces and the agents themselves.


\subsubsection{Model Rules}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:model-rules}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The rules of a model provide the necessary conditions for emergent behaviours to occur. To simplify things a bit, let’s separate the rules into 3 different categories and look at each one individually:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Restrictive Rules

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Interaction Rules

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Behavioural Rules

\end{enumerate}


\paragraph{Restrictive Rules}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:restrictive-rules}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Restrictive rules can be thought of \textendash{} as the name suggests \textendash{} as any model rules that restrict the model’s components in some way.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The use of restrictive rules can be for a number of reasons, but the 2 main reasons that you will typically be creating these rules for are: to simplify the model, and to ensure that the model is accurate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When there is a need to simplify a model so that it can run more efficiently, it may be possible to do this by reducing the number of attributes, but this will usually not have much of an effect as
attributes do not cause much of an impact to memory usage or runtime.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Instead, restrictive rules can be created to reduce or completely remove specific behaviours from the model. This is much more likely to lead to performance gains, as behaviours require interactions
between agents to occur, and if the behaviour is not of particular interest, then the number of interactions can be reduced.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The other case when you would likely want to introduce restrictive rules is when the problem definition itself requires these restrictions to be more accurate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A good example of this happens in Schelling’s model, where agents can only move into empty spaces. Given that you want the model to be representative of real life, then it would not make sense
for the people in one household to be able to move into a household that is already occupied.


\paragraph{Interaction Rules}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:interaction-rules}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Rules to do with interactions are primarily used for maintaining the accuracy of the model, and computationally defining the nature of the problem.

\sphinxAtStartPar
As previously mentioned, there are 2 major types of interactions in an \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} that we are interested in: agent\sphinxhyphen{}agent interactions, and agent\sphinxhyphen{}space interactions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
When we are defining how agent\sphinxhyphen{}agent interactions may occur, there are a number of variables to consider for any particular agent, such as:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
What other agents can it interact with?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
When will these interactions happen?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
What attributes/information are needed for this interaction to happen?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
What is the purpose of this interaction?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Which outcomes are expected from this interaction?

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Obviously, your considerations don’t have to be limited to these, as these are highly dependent on your specific model. But these provide a good foundation for the rules you will be designing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In Schelling’s model, the rules of interaction are relatively simple: at every model iteration, each agent looks at its immediate neighbours and observes what group they belong to.

\sphinxAtStartPar
But nowadays, models will rarely be this straightforward… If we use Schelling’s model as the example, but extend on it to include more information, we can quickly see how
rules of interactions can get complicated.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If instead of being 2 groups in the community, there were 20, and each of these groups had a different level of social interaction, then the rules of interaction would be different. Instead,
when it comes time to observe neighbours, agents from one group might only look at their immediate neighbours, but agents from another group would want to look at their neighbour’s neighbours as
well, and so on.

\sphinxAtStartPar
There may also exist interaction rules for agent\sphinxhyphen{}space interactions, which would take into account similar questions when being defined. The only difference being that rather than looking
at an agent in the context of other agents, we are looking at the agent in the context of their environment.

\sphinxAtStartPar
And so, the rules of interaction that are defined for your model must take these things into consideration, so that you can decide how strict and specific you want to design these rules to be.


\paragraph{Behavioural Rules}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:behavioural-rules}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, we have behavioural rules, which determine the way in which agents and the environment react to interactions and changes in conditions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Similar to interaction rules, behavioural rules will typically be aiming to ensure the accuracy of the model and the phenomenon being simulated.
And these rules may also be applied differently depending on how the agent is reacting to other agents (agent\sphinxhyphen{}agent) versus how they are reacting
to their environment (agent\sphinxhyphen{}space).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given that behavioural rules outline the ways that agents will react to a changing situation, these are where there is most potential for impact to
the model’s emergent behaviours.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In Schelling’s model, the behavioural rules are simple again: after following the rules of interaction and observing their neighbours, each agent then
determines if there are enough agents that belong to their same group before deciding if they will move.


\paragraph{Random or Deterministic?}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:random-or-deterministic}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Regardless of which type of rule we are talking about, an important decision that must be made when defining them is whether the rule will follow a random
or deterministic process.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Again, this decision strongly depends on your particular problem, and the computational resources that you have available,

\sphinxAtStartPar
Stochastic (random) processes will mean a larger computational overhead as a large number of random values and thresholds will have to be drawn each time that
a rule is applied to an agent.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Whereas deterministic rules will simply use the same values and thresholds each time.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The big difference between stochastic or deterministic rules comes down to the model’s explanatory power and the nature of the problem.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Some phenomena in nature (e.g. radioactive decay) are entirely stochastically determined, and would require stochastic processes to model them accurately.

\sphinxAtStartPar
And there are also other problems that aren’t inherently random by nature, but they are better explained when some components within them are stochastically
determined (e.g. social interactions).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For some models, such as Schelling’s, the use of deterministic thresholds and values is enough to produce valid emergent behaviours that align with what is
seen in reality.


\subsubsection{Emergent Behaviours}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:emergent-behaviours}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You may have noticed that throughout the previous sections, we have kept mentioning the idea of “emergent behaviour”, so let us explore it in more detail.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Definition:} Emergent behaviour is any behaviour of interest that is produced as a final outcome of the agent\sphinxhyphen{}based modelling process.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If we use the traditional terminology of the scientific method, you could then say that “emergent behaviours” in an \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} are equivalent
to the dependent variable (i.e. the results that are being analysed).

\sphinxAtStartPar
In most cases of \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM}, you will be designing you model around an established problem, with a somewhat clear expectation of
what behaviours are expected as an outcome, and an idea of what outcomes would be nonsensical and outright impossible following common sense.

\sphinxAtStartPar
However, there may be some cases where the outcome is not clearly defined, because the process that is being modelled has too many variables to accurately
predict. A good example of this in real life are opinion polls prior to federal elections. In many cases, the polls may indicate that it is a “certainty”
for candidate A to win the election, but then for some reason or another, candidate B ends up winning.

\sphinxAtStartPar
And this is due to multiple factors. It could be possible that by chance, the people polled were just not representative of all voters. Candidate A may
have catastrophically blundered and lost voter support between the polls and the election. Or the elections may have been rigged.

\sphinxAtStartPar
But, \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABMs} have never been intended to be used to create deterministic predictions, rather they are used as tools to better
simulate and understand the processes behind the behaviours, and how these can be affected by different factors.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Approaching the problem from this perspective, the real utility of an \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM} comes from its ability to deeply explore and
understand the process rather than the outcome itself.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is much more interesting to be able to simulate the weeks leading up to the election to see how political propaganda and the candidates’ actions
affected the opinions of the voters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Then assuming that the model is accurate, if the final results don’t reflect what really happened in the election, we can start exploring possible
explanations such as electoral fraud.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Although, this doesn’t mean that \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABMs} couldn’t be used as predictive tools to some extent. Simply knowing how certain
conditions have historically impacted behaviours is enough information to be able to change those behaviours in the future.

\sphinxAtStartPar
We can also use these models to simulate hypothetical conditions, and then see what types of behaviours emerge from those conditions; which then allows
us to preemptively avoid conditions leading to “negative outcomes”, or foster conditions leading to “positive outcomes”.


\paragraph{How to tell if behaviours have emerged}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:how-to-tell-if-behaviours-have-emerged}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Now that you’ve seen what emergent behaviour is and what it means in the overall scheme of \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM}, you may be asking yourself
“How can I tell when emergent behaviours appear?”.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given that emergent behaviours are treated as the dependant variable in your model, it is not enough to simply say that any and all outcomes of the model
are “emergent behaviours” in and of themselves.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Rather, you should be defining a model outcome as an “emergent behaviour” based on its usefulness towards explaining your dependant variable(s).

\sphinxAtStartPar
And typically, emergent behaviour is easy to detect. Almost all model outcomes that can be defined as emergent behaviours will: be directly or indirectly, but
closely related to you dependant variable(s), separate agents into distinct “behavioural groups”, and have clearly detectable patterns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Using Schelling’s model as an example, the emergent behaviour is clearly seen to be the formation of homogeneous group neighbourhoods. This progressive
homogeneity is directly related to the dependant variable (segregation), separates the agents into distinct groups (the different neighbourhoods), and
has a clearly detectable pattern (the agents start to have more and more neighbours belonging to their own group).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Despite emergent behaviours typically being clear to see, it is important to not become “tunnel\sphinxhyphen{}visioned” into a strict preconception of what the emergent
behaviour “should” look like. If you focus too much on what you are expecting to see, then it becomes easy to miss emergent behaviours that \textendash{} while equally
valid \textendash{} are not what you were expecting.


\subsubsection{The Scientific Method}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:the-scientific-method}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In relation to this last point, it is worth briefly touching on the “scientific method”, and the general ways in which you should be aiming to carry out
you research.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It has become increasingly common in academia to relentlessly pursue “significant” results that agree with some initial hypotheses. This is not how research
should be carried out.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is important to have your initial hypotheses to inform you about how to design your experiments, and the approach that you want to take in your
methodology. Your initial hypotheses will also give you a good starting point for a literature review, and the areas of past research that you should focus on.

\sphinxAtStartPar
But once your experiments have been designed, you should completely forget about your hypotheses until you are analysing your results. That is to say,
you should not start cherry\sphinxhyphen{}picking data points and constantly changing your model because you are not satisfied with the results you are getting.

\sphinxAtStartPar
You should instead try to be as neutral as possible, and interpret the results with the least amount of bias as possible. Even if you do not agree with
the results, that doesn’t change the fact that those results reflect reality, and denying or altering those results is the same as denying the reality
we live in.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Results that directly go against your initial hypotheses, or simply do not provide strong support for them, are still valid and important results
nonetheless. Knowing what \sphinxstyleemphasis{isn’t} true is equally as useful as knowing what \sphinxstyleemphasis{is}…


\subsubsection{Analysing Your Final Results}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:analysing-your-final-results}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When it comes to analysing your final results, there are a number of ways that this can be done, and it depends on what your particular needs are.

\sphinxAtStartPar
In broad terms, there are two main ways that you would be analysing the results of your \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM}: statistical methods, and
visualisations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Although, you will likely be using both of these methods together, and there will always be a similar basic order of analysis that you will be
following:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Define all relevant data that you need or want from your results

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Collect this data during and after the model’s runtime

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Perform an initial, basic exploratory analysis

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Look for any obvious initial patterns or trends to inform further analysis

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Carry out more complicated statistical and visual analyses

\end{enumerate}
\begin{quote}

\sphinxAtStartPar
5.1. Possibly include specific analytical tests that have been established in literature
5.2. Include any other tests or explorations that are specific to your problem
\end{quote}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finally, gather all your observations and start to describe your findings

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This isn’t set in stone, and you can approach the analysis of your results however works best for you, but this is a good starting point for the
majority of cases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Now let’s look into the statistical methods and visualisations that you might be using for your analysis in a bit more detail.


\paragraph{Statistical Methods}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:statistical-methods}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Statistical methods will probably be the foundation of your analysis in most cases, as these use concrete mathematical equations and the quantitative data
produced by your model to produce definitive metrics and significant conclusions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The most basic of the statistical tests, which can be used for your initial exploratory analysis, are the descriptive statistics:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Mean} (\(\mu\)) = \(\frac{1}{n}(\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1}x_{i})\) = sum of all values / number of values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Median} = The value that appears at the exact middle of a set of values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Mode} = The value that appears the most frequently in a set of values

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Standard Deviation} (\(\sigma\)) = \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1} (x_{i} - \mu)^{2}}\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Quartiles} = Splitting the data into evenly sized subsets

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These initial statistics provide you with enough information to be able to see any obvious patterns in the data, or areas which are in need of more detailed
analysis to provide useful results.

\sphinxAtStartPar
From these basic statistics, we can then go into more detailed metrics or tests which are chosen depending on the information you got from this first step.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Below we’ll briefly go over some of the more commonly encountered complex statistical methods:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{KMeans Clustering:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
KMeans clustering is a method which is defined through the mathematical equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\underset{S}{\arg\min}\sum\limits^{k}_{i=1}\sum\limits_{x\in S_{i}}||x - \mu_{i}||^{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\mu_{i}\) is the mean of the points in cluster \(S_{i}\), defined by:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mu_{i} = \frac{1}{|S_{i}|}\sum\limits_{x\in S_{i}}x\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
In simple terms, the KMeans equation is looking for the values of clusters S which minimise the variance (\(\sigma^{2}\)) present
across all clusters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The main use of clustering in your analysis will be to determine if there are any major “groups” formed within the output data, and how well the
output data actually separates itself into those groups.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If after performing clustering on the data, there is very little variance across the determined clusters, then you can be more confident that there
are clear differences between the groups in the data.

\sphinxAtStartPar
On the other hand, if the algorithm has trouble converging on a solution, or whatever solutions it proposes have a very high variance, it cannot be
said that the output data is significantly heterogeneous.

\sphinxAtStartPar
It is also worth noting that clustering can be used when constructing the initial model in some cases; allowing for the initial population of agents
to be simplified into aggregate groups for simulation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Chi\sphinxhyphen{}Squared} (\(\chi^{2}\)) \sphinxstylestrong{Tests:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\chi^{2}\) tests are primarily used for null\sphinxhyphen{}hypothesis testing, in which one looks at how likely it is for an observed result to have been produced
assuming that some initial hypothesis were true.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The most widely used of the \(\chi^{2}\) tests is Pearson’s \(\chi^{2}\) test, whose test statistic is calculated through the following equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\chi^{2} = N \sum\limits^{n}_{i=1}\frac{(O_{i}/N - p_{i})^{2}}{p_{i}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\chi^{2}\) = Pearson’s cumulative test statistic

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(O_{i}\) = the number of observations of type \(i\)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(N\) = the total number of observations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(p_{i}\) = the theoretical probability of type \(i\) appearing under the null hypothesis

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n\) = the total number of types

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Once you have calculated the \(\chi^{2}\) test statistic, you compare it against the \(\chi^{2}\)\sphinxhyphen{}distribution with the appropriate degrees of
freedom, and see how far away from the center of that distribution the test statistic is.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If the test statistic is far enough away from the center of the distribution (the 95th percentile is the typical cutoff used), then there is evidence
that the observed results are statistically significantly different from those that would be produced under the null hypothesis.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \(\chi^{2}\) test can also be used in combination with clustering, and you can further confirm that the clusters generated by the algorithm
are indeed significantly different from each other.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Log Odds:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You may already be familiar with probability (\(p\)), which is a measure of how likely it is for some event to occur, or some value to appear in
a population.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The probability can be further extended into “odds”, which are the relative ratio of the probability being true versus it being false, and is defined
as \(\frac{p}{1-p}\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
The log odds, as the name would suggest, are produced by simply applying the natural logarithm to the odds:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}logodds(p) = \ln(\frac{p}{1-p})\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The log odds provide the same fundamental information as the traditional odds \textendash{} which is the relative ratio of p being true versus p being false.

\sphinxAtStartPar
But the benefit to using log odds over traditional odds is that it allows for a much more detailed comparison of odds values, especially in situations
where the traditional odds may take extreme values (very small or very large).


\paragraph{Visualisations}
\label{\detokenize{user/abs_beginners:visualisations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Visualisations can play a complementary role in the initial exploratory analysis, but they are most useful for contextualising and clarifying the
exploratory statistics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
While you can realistically visualise pretty much any result, in the case of \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABMs} you will likely be creating visualisations
which can be categorised into one of two broad groups.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Model Visualisations:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Model visualisations are the more unique type of visualisations that can be generated from an \sphinxstyleabbreviation{ABM}, and are probably what you
are thinking of when you hear about visualisations in this context.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Statistic Visualisations:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Statistic visualisations, on the other hand, don’t necessarily provide any new information, but they extend on what you can see in the generated statistics.

\subsection{gatoh.graphs.Graph.calculate\_polarisation}
\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.graphs.Graph.calculate_polarisation:gatoh-graphs-graph-calculate-polarisation}}\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.graphs.Graph.calculate_polarisation::doc}}\index{calculate\_polarisation() (Graph method)@\spxentry{calculate\_polarisation()}\spxextra{Graph method}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.graphs.Graph.calculate_polarisation:gatoh.graphs.Graph.calculate_polarisation}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Graph.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_polarisation}}}
{}
{{ $\rightarrow$ float}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculates the level of opinion polarisation in this {\hyperref[\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.graphs.Graph:gatoh.graphs.Graph}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Graph}}}}} based on the equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\pi(k) = \frac{1}{|K|(|K| - 1)}\sum_{i \neq j}^{i \in K, j \in K}(d_{ij} - y)^{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(K\) is the set of agents within this Graph, \(d_{ij}\) is the distance between
the opinions of agents \(i\) and \(j\), and \(y\) is the mean opinion distance among
all agents in this Graph.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The measure of opinion radicalisation in this social hierarchy.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
float

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}


\sphinxstepscope

A function that will use the betweenness centrality measures of the nodes in the graph
to separate them into a specific number of clusters.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This function uses:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
KMeans as the main clustering algorithm

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Dijkstra all\sphinxhyphen{}pairs path lengths for the distances between nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Betweenness centrality for the KMeans evaluation metric when determining centers

\end{itemize}
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{k}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The number of clusters to separate the graph into.

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}

A helper class that allows rustworkx to more efficiently store information about Agent relationships in the graph edges.
As the social hierarchies are assumed to be DiGraphs, each GraphEdge is directional, and the social weighting that Agent
A places on Agent B will not necessarily be equally reciprocated.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{hierarchy}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{str}}) \textendash{} The name of the social hierarchy that this edge belongs to.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsection{gatoh.graphs.GroupGraph.calculate\_polarisation}
\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.graphs.GroupGraph.calculate_polarisation:gatoh-graphs-groupgraph-calculate-polarisation}}\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.graphs.GroupGraph.calculate_polarisation::doc}}\index{calculate\_polarisation() (GroupGraph method)@\spxentry{calculate\_polarisation()}\spxextra{GroupGraph method}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.graphs.GroupGraph.calculate_polarisation:gatoh.graphs.GroupGraph.calculate_polarisation}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GroupGraph.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_polarisation}}}
{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{hierarchy}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{str}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{default_value}{\textquotesingle{}\textquotesingle{}}}}
{{ $\rightarrow$ float}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculates the level of opinion polarisation in this {\hyperref[\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.graphs.GroupGraph:gatoh.graphs.GroupGraph}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{GroupGraph}}}}} based on the equation:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\pi(k) = \frac{1}{|K|(|K| - 1)}\sum_{i \neq j}^{i \in K, j \in K}(d_{ij} - y)^{2}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(K\) is the set of groups within this GroupGraph, \(d_{ij}\) is the distance between the
opinions of groups \(i\) and \(j:, and :math:`y\) is the mean opinion distance among all groups
in this GroupGraph.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The measure of opinion radicalisation in this social network.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
float

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

Bases: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{object}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A helper class that allows rustworkx to more efficiently store information about Group relationships in the graph edges.
As the social hierarchies are assumed to be DiGraphs, each GroupEdge is directional, and the aggregate weighting that
the Agents in group A place on those in group B will not necessarily be equally reciprocated.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{hierarchy}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{str}}) \textendash{} The name of the social hierarchy that this edge belongs to.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{from\_node}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The index of the origin node.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{to\_node}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The index of the destination node.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{weighting}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{optional}}) \textendash{} The aggregate relationship opinion value that is being assigned (range {[}\sphinxhyphen{}1, 1{]}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{rw\_params}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{tuple}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{optional}}) \textendash{} The normal distribution (mean, variance) to assign for relationship\sphinxhyphen{}specific random walk effects.

\end{itemize}

\end{description}\end{quote}

\subsection{gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate\_density}
\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_density:gatoh-model-abmodel-calculate-density}}\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_density::doc}}\index{calculate\_density() (ABModel method)@\spxentry{calculate\_density()}\spxextra{ABModel method}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_density:gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_density}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ABModel.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_density}}}
{}
{{ $\rightarrow$ float}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate the density of the entire network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The density of a graph is defined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D = \frac{l}{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
which simply refers to the proportion of existing relationships versus the total possible relationships.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Given that gatoh is multilayer, and bidirectional relationships can exist,
the density calculation must instead be defined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}D = \frac{l}{\sum n(n-1)}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where the summation is the total possible relationships across all layers.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The density metric for the entire social network.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
float

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}


\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate\_interdependence}
\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_interdependence:gatoh-model-abmodel-calculate-interdependence}}\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_interdependence::doc}}\index{calculate\_interdependence() (ABModel method)@\spxentry{calculate\_interdependence()}\spxextra{ABModel method}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_interdependence:gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_interdependence}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ABModel.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_interdependence}}}
{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{layer}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{int}}}
{{ $\rightarrow$ float}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate the layer interdependence; a measure of how much impact a specific layer has in the overall
social network.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The general formula for layer interdependence is defined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\lambda^{a} = \frac{\sum_{i}\sum_{j \neq i}\Psi^{a}_{ij}}{\sum_{i}\sum_{j \neq i}\Psi_{ij}}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(\Psi^{a}_{ij}\) describes the number of shortest paths between nodes \(i\) and \(j\)
using two or more layers, where at least one of the layers passed through is \(a\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
For the case of multilayer social contagion modeling, it has been defined here as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\lambda^{a} = \frac{\sum_{i}\sum_{j \neq i}|OC'_{i}(j)^{a}|}{\sum_{i}\sum_{j \neq i}|OC'_{i}(j)|}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
where \(|OC'_{i}(j)^{a}|\) is Agent \(j\)’s opinion climate value as perceived by Agent \(i\)
in the social hierarchy layer \(a\). Although, the absolute of this value should be taken, as this
is representative of the real “strength” of a layer.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{layer}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}) \textendash{} The index of the layer of interest.

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The layer interdependence measure for the layer of interest.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
float

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}


\sphinxstepscope

\subsection{gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate\_navigability}
\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_navigability:gatoh-model-abmodel-calculate-navigability}}\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_navigability::doc}}\index{calculate\_navigability() (ABModel method)@\spxentry{calculate\_navigability()}\spxextra{ABModel method}}

\begin{fulllineitems}
\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{apiref/gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_navigability:gatoh.model.ABModel.calculate_navigability}}
\pysigstartsignatures
\pysiglinewithargsret
{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ABModel.}}\sphinxbfcode{\sphinxupquote{calculate\_navigability}}}
{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{from\_node}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{tuple\DUrole{p}{{[}}int\DUrole{p}{,}\DUrole{w}{ }int\DUrole{p}{{]}}}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{to\_node}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{tuple\DUrole{p}{{[}}int\DUrole{p}{,}\DUrole{w}{ }int\DUrole{p}{{]}}}}}
{{ $\rightarrow$ float}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Calculate the difficulty of navigating from an arbitrary node \(s\) in some layer \(a\) to another arbitrary
node \(t\) in some layer \(b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) may or may not be the same layer.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The general formulae for the navigatability are defined by:
\begin{align*}\!\begin{aligned}
S(s \rightarrow t) = -\log_{2}\sum_{\{p(s,t)\}} P[p(s,t)]\\
P[p(s,t)] = \frac{1}{k_{s}} \prod_{j \in p(s,t)} \frac{1}{k_{j} - 1}\\
\end{aligned}\end{align*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Although, the relationships across the layers in gatoh are bidirectional and weighted, and as such,
\(P[p(s,t)]\) is redefined as:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}P[p(s,t)] = \frac{w_{s \rightarrow j_{o}}}{k_{s}} \prod_{j \in p(s,t)} \frac{w_{j \rightarrow j + 1}}{k_{j} - 1}\end{split}
\end{equation*}\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{from\_node}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{tuple}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} (agent\_index, graph\_index) for the starting node.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{to\_node}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{tuple}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{[}}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{int}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{{]}}}) \textendash{} (agent\_index, graph\_index) for the end node.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The navigability value for the specified path.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
float

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}


\sphinxstepscope

{\sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{input\_value}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{float}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{a}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{default_value}{0.9}}\sphinxparamcomma \sphinxparam{\DUrole{n}{b}\DUrole{p}{:}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{n}{float}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{o}{=}\DUrole{w}{ }\DUrole{default_value}{0.9}}}
{{ $\rightarrow$ float}}
\pysigstopsignatures
\sphinxAtStartPar
Takes an input value and rescales it using a beta distribution. This function is intended to be used exclusively
for the attenuation of indirect neighbouring opinions when an agent is estimating an opinion climate in a hierarchy.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Importantly, the output values are not used for constructing the opinion climate, instead they serve as a threshold
used to decide if the original opinion values are included or not.

\sphinxAtStartPar
a and b should generally be equal to each other and less than 1.0 to approximate a binomial distribution whose PDF still has
non\sphinxhyphen{}zero values in the range (0, 1). This is to enable modeling of the tendency for opinions to become polarised over time;
with this distribution meaning that agents will place much higher importance on extreme observed opinions and less importance
on moderate opinions.
\begin{quote}\begin{description}
\sphinxlineitem{Parameters}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{input\_value}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}) \textendash{} The value to be attenuated. Should always be in the range {[}\sphinxhyphen{}1, 1{]}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{a}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{optional}}) \textendash{} The alpha parameter for the beta distribution.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleliteralstrong{\sphinxupquote{b}} (\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{float}}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{, }}\sphinxstyleliteralemphasis{\sphinxupquote{optional}}) \textendash{} The beta parameter for the beta distribution.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxlineitem{Returns}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The attenuated input value.

\sphinxlineitem{Return type}
\sphinxAtStartPar
float

\end{description}\end{quote}

\end{fulllineitems}

\section{0.1.0\sphinxhyphen{}alpha}
\label{\detokenize{changelog:id10}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This is the first official release of GATOH.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The main purpose of this release is to start preparing the code and its
supplementary materials for publication as a proper package.


\subsection{New Features}
\label{\detokenize{changelog:id11}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Start of the creation of documentation material. This includes:

\sphinxAtStartPar
index.rst

\sphinxAtStartPar
license.rst

\sphinxAtStartPar

Developer and user manuals

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Getting Started section

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
CITATION.cff

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Mostly working functionality across all main package modules

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Basic model visualisation functionality

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for four commonly used random graph generation algorithms:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
small\sphinxhyphen{}world

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
scale\sphinxhyphen{}free

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
random

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
stochastic blockmodel

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Support for random generation of \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Agent}} objects

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A working data persistence system that allows for loading and saving any models
created with the framework

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Design and implementation of five framework validation experiments

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Initial prototype for a future case study experiment

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Implementation of unit tests for all core module functionalities

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Enforcing of consistent type checking across modules

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Full docstring coverage across the existing code

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Changed the way that default names were generated for model config files to
ensure functionality across different operating systems

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Initial, basic conversion of some Python modules to Rust code. This will likely
be expanded on in the future, with the package adopting a hybrid approach, and
resource\sphinxhyphen{}intensive modules being ported to and optimised in Rust.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Random\sphinxhyphen{}walk mechanisms used to simulate the dynamic nature of agent relationships
in social networks, as well as the variable attitude of agents towards the different
social networks.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Publication of the package code to Zenodo

\end{itemize}


\subsection{Fixes}
\label{\detokenize{changelog:id12}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fixed the way that \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{radicalisation()}} was determining agent
radicalisation for “rational” personality types. Now, the function should properly use the
“aggregate benefit” of neighbours rather than the agent’s personal benefit.
